Kimberley Psych Hospital

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
12 years, a billion rand, many health MECs and contractors invested...and the largest psychiatric hospital in the Sourthen hemisphere remains at least another billion rands away from completion.

Summary:
Originally budgeted at R290-million, a massive state psychiatric hospital – the largest in the southern hemisphere – has stumbled from one construction crisis to another while mental patients in dire need of care rot in prison or face the stigma and threat of living in communities who don't understand them and have little compassion for their condition. The grandiose project outside Kimberley, meant to serve the entire northern region of the Cape and Free State, on which almost a billion rand has already been spent, ground to a halt in 2009 when contractual disputes erupted between the developers and the Northern Cape’s health and public works departments. In 2012 new congtractors were appointed, but progress remains halting as the new contractors INYATSI CONSTRUCTION went bankrupt and were bought out by multi-national construction firm MOTA-ENGIL. The real victims are the state patients who have been kept in prison for years – without having been found guilty of any crime – because the health department has nowhere else to place them. The department has been warned that it could face substantial legal claims from patients who have been deprived of care and freedom, some for as long as 15 years.


Further information:
Inyatsi Construction took over construction in January 2012 - but now they've been replaced by a Portuguese company Mota-Engil SA, who is the main contractor.

According to a presentation by Mota-Engil to a parliamentary group who visited the building site, construction could either be complete by end 2016 by doubling the number of workers on site and raising the monthly bill from R7-million to R35-million or extending the completion date to end 2016. The original deadlines of 2015 have come and gone.

There have even been suggestions to just stop the whole thing and break down the structure but that may be even more expensive and would not resove the problem of what to do with the region's psychiatric patients -- in a province with the highest youth suicide rates.

The majority of the province’s state patients have to wait for placement in prison, without the benefit of any therapy. There is no facility to provide 72-hour assessments of emergency cases, causing logjams in court if cases cannot proceed until the accused have been assessed.

Press Release:


Kimberley Mental Health Hospital
Twelve years in the making and some say, R1-billion over budget, a grandiose construction - meant to be the largest psychiatric hospital in the southern hemisphere - has become the subject of ongoing forensic inquiries and finger-pointing in Kimberley. Psychiatric facilities in the province are desperately lacking — patients await hospital placement in prison because the health department has too few beds in existing hospitals. Why has this ambitious project gone from one building fiasco to the next? And is it still even relevant after psychiatric guidelines changed in the decade since its genesis? Carte Blanche investigates.

 

Script:


VO SCRIPT_Kimberley = 10’00"
 
Sarah Jacobs seldom has someone to talk to about her thirty-year old son. 
SARAH JACOBS: He takes his pills, then he doesn’t want them anymore. He says I want to kill him. he says people are telling him not to take the pills. Voices he hears. CLAIRE MAWISA: In his head? LINDA: yes. 
Johan was eighteen when the frightening hallucinations started.
SARAH JACOBS: he started undressing, running naked into the street, saying Mommy, Im’ going crazy. I don’t know what’s going on — so we took him to hospital and the doctor said it was psychosis.
John’s since been admitted with chronic schizophrenia to Kimberley’s small Psychiatric Hospital. 
SARAH JACOBS: He used to say, Mom you wont ever have to work — one day I’ll play cricket for South Africa. To think he had a grand vision or himself and us.
Based on policy guidelines, the province lacks four to five hundred beds. One of three psychiatrists, adolescent and child specialist Keith Kirimi, was the last psychiatrist recruited a decade ago. 
KEITH KIRIMI: Quite a few patients end up being at home or on the streets — acutely ill patients, suicidal patients, patients who are psychotic, aggressive, violent, committing crimes because they are in psychotic states.
When beds are needed, John sometimes gets to come home.
SARAH JACOBS: I was busy in the house, and he hit me. I ran across to the neighbours. He got me there and beat me. I thought I would die that day. When the police came my daughter asked him, do you know what you did to mom — he had no idea what he’d done. 
John still has his freedom, but many patients await placement in prison, some for years. Provincial deputy DA chairperson Karen de Kock reported the matter to the Human Rights Commission.
KAREN DE KOCK: If these people had the right medicine at the right time, in other words, if there were enough acute beds in the province, many of them would never have committed crime in the first plaCommissionce.  
Last year the Human Rights Commission found the Health Department in breach of their Constitutional duty — and ordered them to make a plan.
SARAH JACOBS: Many people don’t know his condition. I’m scared they will kill him. The friends he sees burn him with cigarettes. They kick him and they don’t want to fetch drugs themselves, so they send him. Because they know if he gets caught, he’s not right. 
Provincial politics has severely affected the plight of psychiatric patients. In 2011 Carte Blanche exposed a number of government projects born in the the era of John Block’s tenure at Public Works. 
Block was found guilty of corruption last month in a case involving undue benefits he received from his companies getting government work. He's voluntarily resigned as provincial ANC leader.
Against this backdrop, came a plan to build a big mental health facility in 2003. 
CLAIRE MAWISA: A state of the art psychiatric hospital in Kimberley that has been twelve years in the making, still hasn't opened its doors...with initial estimated costs of R300-million to what some say have ballooned to over R1,5-billion. 
Pakes Dikgetsi was an ANC MEC from 1994 till he joined COPE in 2009. He was Finance MEC when the first construction tender was awarded to Vista Park Developers.
PAKES DIKGETSI: Towards 2005 red flags started emerging. The budget over-runs were starting to show at that time and progress was beginning to slow down. As treasury we would receive progress reports. We were actually mislead. 
Incomplete site preparation meant Andrew Scholtz’s Vista Park Developers couldn’t even start for six months. 
ANDREW SCHOLTZ: They made 220 serious changes to that building — we built up to a point and we got to break off. We applied legally for an extension of time. The department have allowed us to stay on site to keep on with our progress and work, but they never paid us for two years. 
CLAIRE MAWISA: There is joint responsibility when it comes to the Kimberley Mental Hospital saga — the DOH sits with the funds, but it is Public Works which has to see the project through. 
The team was mired in controversy. 
Public Works’ John Block signed the 2003 appointment of public works official Tshego Motaung’s Babereki Consulting Engineers in the key job of project manager. Babereki was only registered the year after it got the job. Motaung shared business interests with Block and his wife. 
From Health, the then Hospital CEO Deon Madyo steered the initiative, says forensic consultant Ross Henderson. 
ROSS HENDERSON: Deon then became the HOD — there’s a lot of controversial decisions that he made at that hospital. 
Madyo is still facing corruption charges with Block in a case involving the purchase of over-priced water purifiers by the department. 
By 2009 construction had ground to a halt. 
SCOPA paid a site visit. 
At Public Works, Fritz Keller joined in time to see Vista Park’s contract cancelled. 
FRITZ KELLER: He defaulted — late completion and poor management and poor workmanship. 
ANDREW SCHOLTZ: According to minutes of the last meeting on site...you will find not one sentence referring to poor workmanship. The issue of poor workmanship came after I put a claim to the government. 
Some say at least three buildings were complete enough to be commissioned to relieve pressure on patients. 
Scholtz is suing Public Works for an outstanding R54-million.
Babereki was replaced as project manager but still does engineering on site. 
The building was weather-beaten by the time Inyatsi Construction took over. 
Public Works appointed Gobodo Forensic Investigators who found that Vista Park was never recommended to the tender board — but crucial documents proving how jobs had been awarded were lost. The report hinted at political pressures but offered no proof.
PAKES DIKGETSI: The tender board was a very strange animal — it actually almost operated independently and there wasn’t really much accountability. Documents should be available, but for them to have disappeared suggests to me that there’s some people actually wanting to cover their tracks. 
ROSS HENDERSON: Whatever Vista Park’s position was, whatever Babereki’s appointment was, they are not the cause of the escalation of this. Because remember when Vista Park left and when Babereki left the project was standing at just close to R300-million. It is now far over R2-billion.
PAKES DIKGETSI: The investigations that have been taking place have actually been focusing on the wrong places. These professionals, the project managers, the engineering people, the design people, what is it that they have been paid for?...we will have to investigate why is it that the national Department of Health is so silent, we will have to investigate why the national treasury keeps on being happy to simply give out the money.
GUGULETHU MATLAOPANE: As the Department of Health also we contributed to a certain extent to the delays of the completion of the hospital, because we had to change the specifics to be in line with the new model of our mental facilities.
While adapting to evolving care guidelines, HOD Gugulethu Matlaopane is also overseeing a national health department instruction to reduce beds at the new hospital in favour of beds closer to communities across the province.
GUGULETHU MATLAOPANE: Unfortunately the hospital is already standing. There are new policies, but that doesn’t mean that then you have to demolish and start afresh. 
Health puts the total cost to the tax payer, even after furniture and equipment’s been bought, at R1,2-billion max. 
Last year Inyatsi had financial trouble and was bought out by multi-national construction firm, Mota Engil. Delivery is now promised for end of next year. Mota Engil’s asked for more funds to cope with rising labour costs. 
FRITZ KELLER: Yes it has to be established what went wrong on this project right, but to point the finger now who is at fault, it’s too early to say. CLAIRE: Too early?! FRITZ: Yes. CLAIRE: What do you mean too early, 11 years late? FRITZ: We have to complete the project. 
Meanwhile, with nowhere to send their patients, private psychiatrists have built their own hospital, right across from the construction site.
DR KEITH KIRIMI: We approached the IDC who were quite willing to support an idea of bringing a service to patients who are not recognised.  
But for those reliant on the state, NGOs striving to bring dignity to the lives of psychiatric patients say the new facility will somehow be used.
JANNIE VAN ZYL: With the right medicine, medication and treatment, they can act pure normally in society.
Jannie van Zyl runs the Northern Cape Mental Health Society’s protected village for people with mental disabilities. He keenly keeps an eye on the construction site. 
JANNIE VAN ZYL: It’s very urgent, no matter what we are going to do with it now...but it is very urgent, because for our long-stay patients, we need the facility. 
SARAH JACOBS: It will change my life quite a lot. Then I will know my child is safe, and where he is, and he will be there forever.

metadata.Summary: Originally budgeted at R290-million, a massive state psychiatric hospital – the largest in the southern hemisphere – has stumbled from one construction crisis to another while mental patients in dire need of care rot in prison or face the stigma and threat of living in communities who don't understand them and have little compassion for their condition. The grandiose project outside Kimberley, meant to serve the entire northern region of the Cape and Free State, on which almost a billion rand has already been spent, ground to a halt in 2009 when contractual disputes erupted between the developers and the Northern Cape’s health and public works departments. In 2012 new congtractors were appointed, but progress remains halting as the new contractors INYATSI CONSTRUCTION went bankrupt and were bought out by multi-national construction firm MOTA-ENGIL. The real victims are the state patients who have been kept in prison for years – without having been found guilty of any crime – because the health department has nowhere else to place them. The department has been warned that it could face substantial legal claims from patients who have been deprived of care and freedom, some for as long as 15 years.
metadata.Further information: Inyatsi Construction took over construction in January 2012 - but now they've been replaced by a Portuguese company Mota-Engil SA, who is the main contractor. According to a presentation by Mota-Engil to a parliamentary group who visited the building site, construction could either be complete by end 2016 by doubling the number of workers on site and raising the monthly bill from R7-million to R35-million or extending the completion date to end 2016. The original deadlines of 2015 have come and gone. There have even been suggestions to just stop the whole thing and break down the structure but that may be even more expensive and would not resove the problem of what to do with the region's psychiatric patients -- in a province with the highest youth suicide rates. The majority of the province’s state patients have to wait for placement in prison, without the benefit of any therapy. There is no facility to provide 72-hour assessments of emergency cases, causing logjams in court if cases cannot proceed until the accused have been assessed.
